data.title: <![CDATA[FDA Approves Ilumya for Adults With Active Psoriatic Arthritis]]>
data.description:
FDA has approved Sun Pharma’s Ilumya (tildrakizumab-asmn) for adults with active psoriatic arthritis, the company announced Oct. 30.1 The decision adds a second disease to the label of the interleukin-23 (IL-23) inhibitor, which FDA first approved in 2018 for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.

The expansion extends the product from dermatology into rheumatology, where Sun Pharma estimates that as many as 2.4 million Americans live with the disease.1

“FDA approval of Ilumya for adults with active psoriatic arthritis represents another important innovative medicine milestone for Sun Pharma and builds on the established clinical experience of Ilumya in plaque psoriasis,” said Rick Ascroft, North America CEO, Sun Pharma. “As an IL-23 inhibitor administered exclusively by a healthcare provider, Ilumya is now an option for adults with active psoriatic arthritis who are unable to self-administer treatment or who may benefit from regular in-office care.”1

Sun Pharma is positioning provider administration as the product’s distinguishing feature. The announcement did not address launch timing, pricing or how payers might view an in-office model.

Ilumya is also approved for plaque psoriasis in India, Australia, Canada, China and Japan, and in Europe as Ilumetri, which Almirall markets.1

What data support the approval?

The approval rests on two phase 3 studies, INSPIRE-1 and INSPIRE-2, which compared Ilumya 100 mg with placebo over 52 weeks in adults with active psoriatic arthritis.1 INSPIRE-1 enrolled patients with prior exposure to a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor and INSPIRE-2 enrolled patients without it; together they included more than 800 participants.

The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients achieving at least a 20% improvement in American College of Rheumatology response criteria (ACR20) at week 24, and the company reported in 2025 that both studies met it.2 The announcement did not include ACR20 response rates.

Sun Pharma said the studies identified no new safety signals and that safety was consistent with the drug’s established profile. Upper respiratory tract infections were among the most common adverse reactions in the arthritis studies, and patients should be evaluated for tuberculosis before treatment begins.1

data.title: <![CDATA[Three Levels of Digital Clone Use Cases: Q&A with Hamish Brocklebank]]>
data.description:
One of the most discussed use cases in pharma and biotech for AI is the creation of digital twins. By using massive amounts and data, the technology can create a digital recreation of a real person, which can then be used for various research purposes.

Pharmaceutical Executive spoke with Hamish Brocklebank, founder of Brox.AI, about some of the ways that digital twins are being used within the industry, and where the technology could potentially head in the coming years.

According to him, these twins have a variety of uses. One of the more commonly discussed use cases is for pure research. In this instance, a researcher creates a digital twin and then uses AI to simulate the effect of various molecules and conditions. However, Brocklebank explains that there are other use cases which may provide just as much, if not more, value.

Click for the video version of this inverview!

Pharmaceutical Executive: How quickly are AI digital twins growing in the pharma industry?
Hamish Brocklebank: The short answer is that everyone is trying to use AI to speed up research and development cycles and accelerate broader business operations. What is interesting — and I will try not to turn this into too much of a pitch — is that there are multiple different approaches to this, and the term “digital twin” means very different things depending on who is using it.

We have actually retired the term digital twin in favor of “digital clones,” because the underlying approaches vary significantly. They fall into roughly three categories. The first is traditional research, which does not really involve digital twins at all. The second is what most people in the industry mean when they say digital twin — essentially pure synthetic data, where you are asking an AI to simulate how a doctor or patient might behave. In a simplified sense, you are telling the model to pretend to be a specific type of person and asking how they would respond. That is the approach most of our competitors take, and there are multiple variations of it. The third category — and our approach — is building one-to-one clones of actual individuals, because we are prioritizing high accuracy over convenience.

data.title: <![CDATA[Post-Exposure Prophylaxis Is the Missing Piece: Q&A with Florin Draica]]>
data.description:
While the general public may view the COVID-19 pandemic as a thing of the past, the virus continues to impact a significant number of people each year. Worse yet, many people who get sick with COVID find themselves facing long-term impacts, even after the initial sickness has passed.

Pharmaceutical Executive spoke with Florin Draica, senior vice president of US medical affairs at Shionogi, about the status of the disease and how new treatment methods are still being developed, such as XOCOVA. The FDA-approved medication is designed to be taken after exposure to the virus but before symptoms set in, in order to prevent serious illness.

Dr. Draica spoke about the ongoing impact of COVID, along with the industry’s broader need to start pursuing preventative medicines more often. By doing this, the public health playbook could focus on preventing illness while also treating people who still get sick.

Click for the video version of this interview!

Pharmaceutical Executive: What is the importance of reframing COVID-19 as a preventable event?
Dr. Florin Draica: Let’s start by talking about where we are with COVID-19 today. We tend to look at the disease in retrospect and compare it to what it was in 2020 or 2021 — and we are well beyond that phase. But it is important to recognize that COVID-19 continues to affect millions of Americans every year.

People are still being hospitalized, and an increasingly important area of emerging evidence involves the lasting impact of COVID-19 beyond the initial infection. Multiple studies have shown that people diagnosed with COVID-19 experience increased rates of new-onset conditions, or worsening of existing conditions, across neurologic, cardiovascular, respiratory, and chronic kidney disease categories — and this persists throughout the year following infection.

COVID-19 activity also continues to rise during predictable periods, including summer and winter. The disease remains highly transmissible: up to approximately half of people living with an infected individual will go on to develop COVID-19 themselves.

While vaccination remains critical for prevention, it does not always prevent infection completely. Vaccine effectiveness is also reduced in people with certain conditions, particularly those with impaired immunity, and protection wanes over time.

data.title: <![CDATA[Roundup: BioMarin Licenses Long-Acting Fabry Enzyme Therapy for $70 Million Upfront, Ferring to Acquire Fertility Biotech Gameto in Deal Worth Up to $1.38 Billion]]>
data.description:
Two deals announced this week show established drugmakers adding specialty assets in very different corners of medicine. BioMarin paid $70 million upfront for exclusive worldwide rights to an investigational long-acting therapy for Fabry disease, with up to $405 million in further milestones.1

Ferring Pharmaceuticals signed an agreement to acquire Gameto, a cell-engineering company focused on women’s reproductive health, in a transaction worth up to $1.3825 billion if development, regulatory and commercial milestones are met.2

BioMarin Licenses Long-Acting Enzyme Therapy for Fabry Disease

BioMarin entered an exclusive worldwide license agreement with GC Biopharma and Hanmi Pharm for HM15421/GC1134A, an investigational, long-acting enzyme replacement therapy for Fabry disease, the company announced Oct. 29.1 BioMarin pays $70 million upfront.

GC Biopharma and Hanmi are jointly eligible for up to $405 million in development and commercial milestones, plus tiered royalties on net sales; the royalty rates were not disclosed.1

“This agreement reflects our growing commitment to the Fabry community, building on the acquisition of Amicus earlier this year,” says Alexander Hardy, president and chief executive officer of BioMarin.

Following the ongoing Phase 1/2 study, BioMarin assumes sole responsibility for clinical development, manufacturing and commercialization outside Korea, where GC Biopharma and Hanmi retain commercialization rights.1 The release does not say who funds the current study, and it gives no closing conditions or timeline.1

What is HM15421/GC1134A?

The candidate is a human recombinant alpha-galactosidase A enzyme designed for a longer half-life and better stability, features intended to support subcutaneous dosing. BioMarin says it has the potential to be the first subcutaneous enzyme replacement therapy for Fabry disease.1

<![CDATA[Roundup: Astellas Licenses IL-12 Fusion Protein From Audax in Deal Worth Up to $1.34 Billion, EVERSANA Acquires Health Economics Firm Estima Scientific]]>
data.description:
Two transactions announced this week sit at opposite ends of the biopharma value chain: access to an early-stage immuno-oncology program, and the technology used to show payers what a product is worth.

Astellas Pharma Inc. secured an exclusive option on an investigational cancer therapy from Audax Biosciences Pty Ltd, in a deal valued at up to US$1.34 billion excluding royalties.1 EVERSANA, a commercial services provider to the biopharmaceutical industry, acquired Estima Scientific, a London-based health economics and outcomes research (HEOR) technology company, for undisclosed terms.2

Astellas Gains Option on Audax’s IL-12 Antibody-Cytokine Fusion

Astellas and Audax, an Australian biotechnology company, entered an exclusive option and license agreement for DAX-044, an investigational, immune-targeted interleukin-12 (IL-12) antibody-cytokine fusion for immuno-oncology.1

“By combining Audax’s innovative science with Astellas’ development, manufacturing and commercialization expertise, we hope to advance a potential new treatment option for patients with solid tumors, including cancers where effective immune stimulation remains an important therapeutic challenge,” says Takahiko Iwaya, chief strategy officer at Astellas.

If Astellas exercises the option, it would receive a worldwide license to develop, manufacture and commercialize DAX-044 and assume sole responsibility for those activities. Audax has the option to co-fund and co-promote the drug in Australia and New Zealand.

Exercise is subject to customary conditions, including antitrust clearances.1 Total potential value reaches up to US$1.34 billion, excluding royalties.

Audax would receive US$285 million through an upfront payment and a potential option exercise payment, plus up to US$1.05 billion in development and commercial milestones and tiered double-digit royalties on worldwide net sales if the drug is approved.1 Audax will fund and continue development into a Phase 1 study expected to begin in 2027.1

Why has IL-12 been difficult to develop as a cancer therapy?

DAX-044 uses the AVIKINE antibody-cytokine platform and is designed to concentrate IL-12’s immune-activating activity in the tumor microenvironment while limiting the systemic toxicity that has historically constrained IL-12-based therapy.1 That constraint is documented.
